title: QPay in the City, Tugrik on the Steppe: How Expats Actually Pay for Life in Mongolia
summary: Ulaanbaatar runs on QR payments while the countryside runs on cash. Here's how expats in Mongolia handle both without a local bank account.
body_markdown:
It's minus twenty outside and the windows of the guanz are fogged solid. You've just finished a plate of buuz and a bowl of milk tea, and the woman at the till is holding up a laminated card with a QR code on it, looking at you with the patience of someone who does this forty times a day. Everyone before you in line paid in about four seconds: phone out, scan, done. You're the one digging through a parka for tugrik notes, and the smallest thing you have is a 20,000.


This is the daily texture of money in Ulaanbaatar in 2026. The city has quietly become a QR town, and the gap between how locals pay and how foreigners pay is wider here than almost anywhere else in Asia.


## Ulaanbaatar went digital faster than its reputation did


People arrive in Mongolia braced for a cash economy, because that's what every older guidebook says. Then they land in Ulaanbaatar and find[QPay](https://moretapay.com/networks/qpay) stickers on the counter of nearly every coffee shop, pharmacy, supermarket, and hole-in-the-wall canteen. Locals pay through their banking apps, scanning a QR at the register for everything from a cashmere sweater at the State Department Store to a bag of aaruul from a kiosk. Even small stalls inside Narantuul market increasingly have a QR card taped next to the scales.


The catch is that this ecosystem was built for people with Mongolian bank accounts. The apps locals use sit on top of accounts at Khan Bank, Golomt, TDB, and the rest, and opening one of those as a foreigner typically means residency paperwork, in-person visits, and patience. If you're on a shorter stay, or you've just arrived and your visa situation is still settling, you're locked out of the way the whole city pays. It's the same closed-loop frustration travelers hit in China, where


[the noodle shop would honestly prefer you didn't pay cash](https://moretapay.com/blog/the-noodle-shop-doesnt-want-your-cash-money-mistakes-tourists-keep-making-in-china-2026-11-11)


, except Mongolia has far fewer workarounds built for visitors.


## What your foreign card can and can't do here


International cards do work in Mongolia, but only in a narrow slice of the economy. Larger supermarkets, hotels, and mid-range restaurants in central Ulaanbaatar usually take them. Step outside that zone, into the guanz, the market stall, the neighborhood pharmacy, the driver who picked you up near Sukhbaatar Square, and it's QR or cash, full stop. Card terminals also have a way of being "broken" exactly when you need them, which every expat here learns to translate as "please pay another way."


Then there's the foreign transaction fee problem, plus the mystery of what rate your home bank actually gave you, which you only discover days later on a statement. Expats who lean entirely on a foreign card in Mongolia end up paying a quiet tax on every purchase and still carrying cash as a backup.


This is the gap Moreta Pay was built for. You top up a wallet from your home bank or card in your own currency, then scan the same standard merchant QR codes locals scan. Before you confirm, you see the amount in tugrik, the exchange rate, and the merchant name on your screen. The merchant gets paid instantly in their currency, you never opened a Mongolian bank account, and nothing hides in the fine print.


## The two-wallet rhythm expats settle into


Talk to anyone who has lived in Ulaanbaatar for more than a few months and you'll hear a version of the same system: phone for the city, cash for everything beyond it.


In town, QR covers most of daily life. Groceries, coffee, lunch, the gym, the tailor who takes up your winter trousers. With Moreta Pay handling the QR side, your foreign money stops being a handicap at the register, and you stop planning your week around ATM runs in subzero weather.


But Mongolia is not Ulaanbaatar. The moment you head out, to Terelj for a weekend, to Kharkhorin, to a ger camp in the Gobi, you're back in tugrik-note territory. Countryside guanz, roadside shops, horse guides, families selling airag by the highway, these are cash transactions and will be for a long time. Mobile coverage gets patchy, and even where there's signal, a herder's family business isn't running a QR terminal.


So the practical setup looks like this:


- **Keep a working QR wallet for the city.**


That's where the bulk of your spending happens, and it's where carrying wads of cash is least necessary.


- **Withdraw tugrik before you leave town, not after.**


ATMs thin out dramatically outside the capital and aimag centers. Get cash in Ulaanbaatar, in smaller denominations if you can, because breaking a 20,000 note at a countryside shop is a small social event.


- **Don't hoard cash in the city "just in case."**


Tugrik isn't a currency you want to be stuck converting back in bulk when you leave. Hold what the countryside needs, pay digitally for the rest.


## The stuff nobody warns you about


A few Mongolia-specific wrinkles worth knowing before they catch you at a counter:


**Winter is a payments argument for going cashless.**


Fishing bills out of an inner pocket with numb fingers at an outdoor kiosk in January is genuinely miserable. Scanning a QR through a glove-friendly phone screen is not. Expats who arrive in summer and build cash habits often rebuild them by December.


**Taxis are their own economy.**


Plenty of rides in Ulaanbaatar still happen in unofficial cars flagged from the curb, and those are cash. App-based rides and more formal drivers increasingly settle by QR or transfer, so having both options ready keeps every ride simple.


**Online bookings count too.**


If you're arranging travel through platforms that support QR-based checkout, like Trip.com for flights or hotels, a QR wallet works there the same way it does at a register. Moreta Pay handles those online QR payments too, which matters in a country where a lot of domestic travel gets booked last minute.


**Small notes are social currency in the countryside.**


Exact or near-exact change is appreciated at small shops and ger camps, where nobody wants to hunt for change on a 20,000 note for a 3,000 tugrik purchase.


## Set yourself up before the first fogged-up window


The expats who find Mongolia's money situation easy are the ones who stopped treating Ulaanbaatar like a cash city and the countryside like an afterthought. Sort out your QR life for the capital, keep an honest stack of tugrik for the steppe, and the whole country opens up without a single trip to a bank branch.
